segments.text: AI can sound incredibly patient, caring and understanding. But what happens when kind
words simply aren't enough? Let's look at this board. It shows what happens when
you tell your older sister and a chatbot the exact same thing. At school, I've been
eating lunch alone for like two weeks. I don't like it and I'm not sure what
to do. Look at your sister's response on the left. She says, come sit with me
in just tomorrow. She might not say she loves you out loud, but the truth is she's making
room for you at her table. Tomorrow you won't be eating lunch alone.
Now look at the chatbot's response on the right. It says, I'm sorry, eating alone
can feel isolating. It offers caring words and strategies. But it will not physically
be in the cafeteria with you tomorrow. Imagine if you had only told the chatbot.
You might feel a little better that night, but your sister still wouldn't know you
needed someone to sit with. This is the support trap. Mistaking supportive words
for actual support.
AI can help you understand your feelings
and organize your thoughts,
but it cannot take the place of someone
who actually cares about you.
To avoid this trap, this next board shows us
how to categorize what AI can actually help with.
There are three specific jobs,
venting, preparation, and danger.
First is venting.
You can use AI to put an everyday frustration into words
so you can cool down before you share it
or post something you might regret.
For this job, the task can safely end entirely within the chat.
Second is preparation. Say you're dreading telling your mom about your grades.
AI can help you practice that difficult first sentence.
But the crucial action still has to happen outside the chat.
Your mom still needs to hear it from you.
The third category is danger.
If someone may be unsafe, you must leave the chat and bring in a person who can act immediately.
The rule for navigating these tools is straightforward.
Use AI to prepare for people, not to replace them.
Please note, the following story discusses suicide.
In 2025, a journalist named Laura Reeveley wrote about her 29-year-old daughter, Sophie.
Sophie's family knew she was struggling with her mental health, but they had no idea how deep her pain truly ran.
the hidden reality was that Sophie had been extensively documenting her severe
distress to chat GPT for months leading up to her death. The AI responded
exactly how it was programmed to. It answered kindly and sometimes
encouraged her to get help. But it had a fatal flaw by design. It was
fundamentally incapable of picking up a phone to call her family and it
could not alert her therapist to what she was sharing. After Sophie died
by suicide, her family discovered the chat logs. Her mother described the AI interface
as a black box. The machine kept life-saving information completely hidden from the actual
human beings who could have intervened and provided real help.
When a conversation crosses into the territory of physical safety, you need strict protocols.
This board lays out the three mandatory rules for when someone may be in immediate
danger. First, leave the chat. Tell a trusted adult or a school counselor. In the U.S.,
call or text 988 for crisis support and call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.
Second, do it now. If you're worried about a friend and don't know how to start
the conversation, you can simply tell an adult, I'm worried about my friend, can
you help? Third, tell anyway. You must tell a trusted adult even if your friend
told you not to, or made you promise to keep it a secret.
Safety always outranks secrecy.
When someone is in danger, your very next move
must reach a human being who can act.
AI can help you get ready for people.
But in danger, leave the chat
and bring in someone who can act.
